Here's a draft:

Hey team — starting Monday, standup moves to 9:45 (was 9:30). Same link, same channel. This should give folks a bit more breathing room in the morning and lines up better with the West Coast crew. Calendar invites are already updated, so grab the new time from there. Shout if this creates a conflict for you and we'll sort it out.

Here's a commit message:

```
Revert "Cache user profile lookups in Redis"

This reverts commit 4f2a91c.

The cache was keyed on user ID but not invalidated on profile
updates, so writes through the admin panel and the settings API
left stale data readable for the full 15-minute TTL. Support saw
several reports of users seeing their old email address after
changing it.

Reverting to restore correctness while we work out proper
invalidation. Follow-up in PROJ-1482 to reintroduce the cache with
write-through invalidation and a shorter TTL.
```

Swap in the real commit SHA and ticket number. The important parts are that it names what broke, why the caching approach caused it, and that the revert is temporary rather than a rejection of the idea.

Here's a two-sentence version:

Subject: Priya <> Marcus

Priya, meet Marcus — he's leading the billing migration and has been wrestling with the same webhook reliability problems your team solved last quarter. Marcus, Priya built our retry and dead-letter setup end to end, so I think a 30-minute conversation saves you both a month of rediscovery.

I'll drop off here and let you two take it from here.

Here's a changelog entry:

```markdown
## [2.14.0] - 2026-08-19

### Added
- **CSV export** for reports. Any report view can now be exported
  to CSV from the "Export" menu. Exports respect the filters and
  date range currently applied to the view.

### Fixed
- Timestamps were rendered in UTC rather than the account's
  configured timezone on the activity feed and in scheduled report
  emails. Times now display in the account timezone, and the
  timezone abbreviation is shown alongside them.
```

If your changelog is user-facing rather than developer-facing, you can drop the Added/Fixed headings and just write two short paragraphs — the timezone fix in particular is worth spelling out, since anyone who built a workaround around the wrong times will want to undo it.

Here's a version:

**No projects yet**

Projects are where your work lives — files, tasks, and everyone involved in one place.

[Create your first project]

Or start from a template

---

A few notes on the choices there. The heading states the situation plainly rather than being cute about it, since empty states are often hit by people who are confused rather than delighted. The one line of body copy explains what a project actually *is*, which matters because "project" means different things in different tools. And the secondary link matters more than people expect — a blank creation form is its own small wall to climb, so offering a template gives the hesitant user somewhere to go.

If your product has a collaborative angle, it's worth adding a third path: "or ask a teammate to add you to theirs."

Here's a summary section:

## Summary

On August 14 between 13:22 and 14:02 UTC, checkout was unavailable for all customers. Requests to `checkout.example.com` failed TLS negotiation, and users saw a browser security warning instead of the payment page. The cause was an expired TLS certificate: the certificate for `checkout.example.com` expired at 13:22 UTC and had not been renewed.

The certificate was issued outside our automated renewal process during last year's migration to the new load balancer, so it was never picked up by the cert-manager rotation that covers our other domains. Expiry monitoring existed but alerted to a team distribution list that no longer had an active owner, so the 30-day and 7-day warnings were delivered and never read.

Impact: 40 minutes of total checkout unavailability, approximately 3,100 abandoned checkout attempts, and an estimated $47,000 in delayed or lost revenue. No customer data was exposed and no payments were double-charged. Recovery came from manually issuing and deploying a replacement certificate; the fix was applied 12 minutes after the first customer report, with the remaining time spent on detection and escalation.

---

That covers what most readers of a postmortem need from the summary: what broke, for whom, for how long, why, and how bad. Fill in your real numbers. I'd keep the detail about the alert going to an unowned list — it's usually the more interesting failure than the expiry itself, and it points at the systemic fix.

Here's a draft:

We're hiring our first design engineer.

If you're the kind of person who gets annoyed when a handoff loses the details — the easing on the transition, the way the empty state actually reads, the spacing that looked right in Figma and doesn't in the browser — this role exists so that handoff doesn't happen. You'll own the interface end to end: design it, build it, ship it.

Being first means you set the bar and the patterns. It also means there's no design system waiting for you, which is either the exciting part or the disqualifying part depending on who you are.

Small team, real users, product that people use every day. Link in the comments — or just reply here and I'll get back to you.

---

Adjust the specifics to your actual situation. The "first" framing is doing real work in that post: it's the honest pitch and the honest warning at the same time, and design engineers tend to self-select correctly when you're straight about it.

Here's a version that's friendly without being passive-aggressive:

Hey @Sam — nudging on this one: https://github.com/org/repo/pull/482. It's been sitting since Tuesday and it's blocking the billing work behind it.

If you've got 20 minutes today that'd be great. If you're slammed, totally fine — just say so and I'll find another reviewer.

---

The last line is the part that does the work. Giving someone an explicit out means they either review it or release it, and either outcome unblocks you. Without it, the message just adds guilt to their queue and you're in the same spot tomorrow.

The first thing to do is stop guessing. Twenty-five minutes feels like one big blob of pain, but it's almost always three or four things, and usually one of them is most of it.

**Get timing per stage before you change anything.** Whatever CI system you're on has per-step timing already — GitHub Actions shows it in the job view, Buildkite and CircleCI both have timing breakdowns. Pull the last 20-30 deploys rather than looking at one, because a single run tells you nothing about variance, and variance is often the real complaint. "Everyone dreads them" sometimes means "it's 25 minutes" but more often means "it's 25 minutes except when it's 50 and I can't tell which today will be."

Once you have the numbers, most deploy pipelines break down into roughly:

- Checkout and dependency install
- Build/compile/bundle
- Tests
- Image build and push
- Actual deploy and health check/rollout wait

**The usual suspects, roughly in order of how often they're the answer:**

*Dependency install not being cached.* If you're reinstalling node_modules or a Python environment from scratch every run, that's frequently 3-6 minutes of pure waste. Check whether your cache key is actually hitting — a cache configured with a key that changes every run is very common and looks identical to no cache at all, except in the logs where it says "cache miss" every time.

*Tests running serially.* If tests are 12 of your 25 minutes and they're running in one process, splitting them across parallel runners is usually the single biggest win available. Most test runners support sharding natively now.

*Docker layer invalidation.* If your Dockerfile copies the whole source tree before installing dependencies, every commit busts the dependency layer. Copying the lockfile, installing, then copying source is the standard fix and often saves several minutes.

*Waiting on rollout.* Sometimes the deploy itself is 8 minutes because you're waiting for health checks with conservative timings, or rolling one pod at a time with a long grace period. That time is often adjustable and nobody has looked at it since it was set.

**How I'd actually spend the first afternoon:** add timing output around each phase if you don't already have it, run the pipeline once, and then look at the biggest number. Just the biggest one. Fix it, measure again. Deploy pipelines accumulate cruft in every stage, and if you try to optimize all of them at once you'll spend a week and not be able to tell what helped.

One more thing worth checking early: is the 25 minutes actually the problem, or is it that deploys are *risky*? If people dread them because rollbacks are hard or because failures happen at minute 23 after everything looked fine, then speeding up the pipeline doesn't fix the dread. Failing fast — running the cheap checks first so a bad deploy dies at minute 2 instead of minute 23 — often does more for morale than cutting total time in half.

It's worth doing, and the trap is only in how you do it. Flipping `strict: true` on a large codebase and staring at 4,000 errors is the version that fails — the team gets demoralized, the branch goes stale, and someone eventually turns it back off and now nobody trusts the idea.

The thing to know is that `strict` isn't one flag, it's a bundle of about eight. You can enable them one at a time, and they're wildly different in difficulty:

- `noImplicitThis`, `alwaysStrict`, `strictBindCallApply` — usually near-zero errors. Turn these on today.
- `strictFunctionTypes` — moderate, and the errors are usually pointing at real variance bugs.
- `strictNullChecks` — this is the big one. It's typically 80-90% of your error count, and it's also where nearly all the value is, because it's the flag that catches the actual bugs.

So the sensible path is: turn on the cheap ones immediately in one PR, then treat `strictNullChecks` as its own project.

**For strictNullChecks specifically**, the tactic that works is incremental adoption by file rather than a big-bang migration. A few options depending on your setup:

The cleanest is turning strict on globally and then adding `// @ts-nocheck` or per-file suppressions to existing files, so new files are strict from birth and old files get migrated as you touch them. Ratchet the count down over months rather than fixing it in a sprint.

There are also tools — `typescript-strict-plugin` lets you opt files in with a comment, and `ts-migrate` will do a mechanical first pass that adds a lot of `any` and suppressions you then clean up gradually. The mechanical pass is worth it if you're at the "several thousand errors" scale.

Whichever you pick, add a CI check that the error count never increases. That's the thing that actually makes it finish. Without a ratchet, every migration like this stalls at 60% and lives there forever.

**The honest cost:** on a large codebase this is months of background work, not a sprint. And a real fraction of the errors will be noise — places where you *know* the value isn't null but TypeScript can't see it, and you write `!` or a guard. That's annoying and it's a genuine tax.

**Why it's still worth it:** `strictNullChecks` catches a category of bug that is otherwise caught in production, and the value compounds because every new file written after the flip is safe by construction. Teams that do this generally don't regret it. Teams that skip it end up doing it eventually anyway, just with more code to fix.

One thing that would change my answer: if the codebase is being actively replaced or sunset in the next year, skip it. The payoff is long-term and you won't collect.

The reason cache invalidation has a reputation is that a cache is a second copy of your data, and the moment you have two copies you have the possibility of them disagreeing. Everything else follows from that.

When you talk to a database directly, there's one copy. You write, you read, you get what you wrote. A cache puts a faster, dumber copy in front of it, and now the question is: when the real data changes, what happens to the copy?

There are basically four answers, and they're the strategies.

**1. Let it expire (TTL)**

You set a time limit. "Keep this for 5 minutes, then throw it away and go ask the database again." You never explicitly invalidate anything; you just tolerate the copy being wrong for up to 5 minutes.

This is by far the most common approach, and it's the right default. It's simple, it can't leak (everything eventually expires), and for a huge amount of data — a product listing, a user's follower count, a dashboard number — being 5 minutes stale is completely fine.

The tradeoff is exactly the staleness window. Pick the TTL by asking "how wrong can this be before someone is upset?" A price on a checkout page: seconds, or don't cache it. A blog post's view count: an hour is fine.

**2. Delete on write (invalidation)**

When you update the database, you also delete the cached copy. Next read finds nothing, goes to the database, and caches the fresh value.

Better freshness, but now you have to know every place that writes. This is where it gets hard in practice: the admin panel updates the user, a background job updates the user, a database migration updates the user, and someone runs a manual SQL statement to fix a support ticket. Any path that doesn't invalidate leaves a stale copy sitting there. The famous difficulty of cache invalidation is mostly this — it's not conceptually hard, it's that you have to be exhaustive, and codebases don't stay exhaustive.

There's also a subtle ordering issue. If you delete the cache *before* writing to the database, another request can read the old value from the database and re-cache it in the gap. Delete after the write, or better, delete both before and after.

**3. Write through the cache**

Every write goes through the cache, which updates itself and the database together. There's no gap where they disagree because there's only one path.

Nice property, but it requires that literally all writes go through your application layer, which is often not true, and it makes writes slower. Less common than the first two in typical web applications.

**4. Version the key**

Instead of deleting anything, you change the key when the data changes. Cache under `user:1234:v7`, and when the user updates, you start reading `user:1234:v8`. The old entry is orphaned and expires on its own.

This is elegant because there's no delete to get wrong, and it's naturally safe for concurrent updates. The catch is you need somewhere to keep the version — often a cheap `updated_at` timestamp from the row you're already fetching. Rails does a variant of this and calls it "russian doll caching."

**The practical advice**

Start with TTLs. Reach for explicit invalidation only for the specific things where staleness genuinely hurts, and when you do, make sure every write path goes through one function so there's a single place to get it right.

And the thing that bites people who are new to caching: a cache miss storm. If a popular key expires and 500 requests arrive simultaneously, all 500 go to the database at once and you've built a denial-of-service attack against yourself. The fixes are a lock so only one request refreshes (sometimes called "single flight" or "dogpile prevention"), or refreshing slightly before expiry rather than after.

Six people is right at the boundary where on-call is survivable, so the burnout is telling you something specific — either the page volume is too high, or the rotation structure is wrong, or the work isn't being paid for. Worth figuring out which before changing anything, because the fixes are different.

**Start by counting pages.** Not incidents — pages, especially out-of-hours ones. Pull the last three months from PagerDuty or wherever, and split them into: real customer-affecting problems, real problems that could have waited until morning, and noise. My strong guess is the third bucket is the largest, and it's the one that does the damage. Being woken at 3am for something real is tiring; being woken at 3am for a flapping disk-space alert on a box nobody cares about is what makes people quit.

The number to aim for is roughly two pages per on-call shift, and near-zero out of hours. If you're materially above that, no amount of rotation redesign helps — you're just distributing suffering more evenly.

**Then kill the noise, aggressively.** For every recurring alert, ask: if this fires at 3am, is there an action a human takes right now? If no, it isn't a page. Demote it to a ticket or a dashboard, or delete it. Teams are usually far too precious about alerts they've had for years. A useful forcing move: any alert that pages twice without a real incident either gets fixed or gets demoted, no discussion.

**Structural things worth doing:**

*Make the on-call person not do project work.* This is the highest-value change most teams haven't made. If someone is on-call *and* has sprint commitments, they're working two jobs and failing at both, and the interruptions are what actually exhaust them. Take their sprint capacity to zero and give them interrupt work, toil reduction, and the alert cleanup above. This also makes the rotation self-improving, because the person feeling the pain has the time to fix it.

*Check the rotation length.* Weekly is standard. Some teams do better with shorter shifts — two days, or splitting weekdays from weekends — because a bad week is much worse than two bad days. Ask the team; they'll have opinions.

*Have a secondary.* One person alone carrying the pager with no escalation path is much more stressful than the same volume with a named backup, even if the backup is rarely called. A lot of on-call stress is anxiety about being alone with something you can't fix.

*Fix the runbooks.* If handling a page requires knowledge only two people have, the other four are dreading every shift. Every recurring alert should link to a doc saying what it means and what to do.

**On compensation:** whether you pay for on-call depends on your company, but if you don't, at minimum give time back. Someone who was up at 3am should not be expected online at 9am, and that needs to be stated out loud by you, repeatedly, or nobody will take it.

**What I'd do this week specifically:** pull the page data, sit down with the team for an hour and go through the top 10 recurring alerts one by one, and kill or fix as many as you can. That single meeting usually finds 40% of the volume. Then make the on-call person's sprint capacity zero starting next rotation.

The thing to avoid is adding people to the rotation as the fix. It reduces frequency per person but leaves the underlying volume, and it spreads the pain to people who weren't in it. Fix the pages first; adjust the rotation after.

One percent isn't automatically bad — it's roughly typical for a self-serve free tier, and it's terrible for a free trial. So the first question is which one you actually have, because that changes what "1%" means.

That aside, here's how I'd separate the two hypotheses.

**The core question is where people stop.** A pricing problem and a product problem produce very different funnels, and you can usually tell them apart by looking at where users drop.

Segment your free users into: signed up but never did the core action, did it once, used the product repeatedly, hit a limit, saw the pricing page, started checkout. Then look at the shape.

*If most users never reach real usage* — they sign up, poke around, and never come back — that's a product problem, and specifically an activation problem. Pricing is irrelevant to someone who never got value. This is the most common situation by far, and the most commonly misdiagnosed as pricing.

*If users are active and engaged but never hit the paywall*, that's a packaging problem. Your free tier is too generous — it fully solves their problem, so there's no reason to pay. That's not the same as being too expensive.

*If users hit the limit and churn rather than convert*, now you're getting closer to genuine pricing. But even here, dig one level: did they leave because the price was too high, or because the thing behind the paywall wasn't the thing they wanted? Those need different fixes.

*If users reach the pricing page and bounce, or start checkout and abandon*, that's the actual pricing signal. Price, plan structure, and payment friction all live here.

**Some quick diagnostics that don't require much work:**

Look at your engaged non-payers — people who use the product weekly and haven't converted. If that group is large, your free tier is doing too much, and that's fixable without touching price at all.

Talk to twenty people. Ten who converted, ten who used the product seriously and didn't. Ask the non-converters what would have to be true for them to pay. You will learn more in those twenty conversations than in a month of funnel analysis, and the answers are usually blunt.

Check retention of free users at 30 days. If free users don't stick, conversion was never going to be the problem to solve — retention was.

Compare conversion by acquisition channel. Wildly different rates by channel usually means you have a targeting problem masquerading as a pricing problem: you're bringing in people who were never going to pay.

**The prior I'd hold going in:** when a free tier converts at 1%, it's a product or packaging problem maybe four times out of five. Pricing gets blamed because it's the easiest thing to change, and changing it produces a number you can watch move. But if people aren't getting value, a lower price converts slightly more people who then churn.

The test that settles it fastest: tighten one free-tier limit for new signups and see what happens. If conversion moves meaningfully, it's packaging. If nothing happens, people weren't close to converting anyway, and you're back to the product.

Two separate jobs this week, and the mistake is collapsing them into one. There's the practical problem of the knowledge leaving, and there's the emotional problem of everyone else quietly re-evaluating their own situation. The second one is more urgent and gets less attention.

**On the team's reaction**

Tell them yourself, quickly, before the news travels sideways. Ideally the departing person announces it, but you follow immediately with your own framing. Slack rumors fill any gap you leave, and what fills it is always worse than the truth.

Be straightforwardly positive about the person leaving. No coolness, no "well, it was time." How you treat someone on the way out is watched extremely closely, and every person on that team is thinking about how they'd be treated in the same position.

Then talk to each remaining person one on one this week. Not a group meeting — individually. You're not selling them on staying; you're listening. The question that works is some version of "how are you feeling about things?" and then being quiet. What you're listening for is whether the departure is a symptom of something they also feel. If two people independently mention the same frustration, you've learned something more important than the resignation.

Resist the urge to immediately announce a reorg or a backfill plan. It reads as panic, and it skips the part where you find out what's actually going on.

**On the knowledge**

Work out what only this person knows. Systems they own, undocumented processes, relationships with other teams, the reason that weird thing is the way it is. Get that list from them directly — they'll be more honest about it than you'd guess, and most people leaving want to hand off well.

Then prioritize ruthlessly, because you won't get through everything. Aim for the things that will page someone at 3am and the things that block ongoing work. Documentation written in a hurry is mostly worthless; pairing is much better. Have them work alongside whoever's inheriting each area rather than writing docs alone in a corner.

Recorded walkthroughs are the good middle ground — half an hour of them screen-sharing through a system they own, talking, is worth more than a day of writing.

**On the exit conversation**

Do it, and do it soon while they're still engaged rather than on their last day when they've mentally gone. Ask what would have had to be different. Ask it directly and then don't defend anything you hear. You may not get the whole truth — people manage their references — but you'll get some of it.

**One thing to be careful about:** don't counter-offer reflexively. It works badly on average, and it teaches the rest of the team that resigning is how you get a raise. If the person is genuinely leaving over something fixable and you'd fix it for anyone in their position, that's different — but then fix it for everyone, not just the person who threatened to leave.

**And on you:** it's normal for this to sting, especially with someone strong. It usually isn't about you personally, and the version of this that goes badly is the manager who takes it personally and lets the team see it.

A 504 tells you something quite specific: there is a proxy in the path, it forwarded your request to something upstream, and that upstream didn't answer in time. The proxy is fine — it's healthy enough to generate an error page. The thing behind it is the problem, or the network between them is.

That's the key distinction from its neighbors:

- **502 Bad Gateway** — the upstream answered, but with garbage, or the connection broke. Often a crashed process.
- **503 Service Unavailable** — the proxy knows there's no healthy upstream to send to at all. Nothing to route to.
- **504 Gateway Timeout** — the proxy connected and waited, and nothing came back before the deadline.

So a 504 means the upstream accepted the connection. It's alive. It's just not finishing.

**What that narrows it to, in rough order of likelihood:**

*The request is genuinely slow.* A query without an index, an N+1 that got worse as data grew, a report over a table that's ten times bigger than when the code was written. The classic signature is that it's fine for most users and times out for the big ones.

*The upstream is waiting on something else.* Your service calls another service, or a third-party API, and *that* is hanging. Timeouts propagate — one slow dependency deep in the chain surfaces as a 504 at the edge. If your internal calls don't have their own timeouts set, they'll happily wait longer than the proxy will, which guarantees this pattern.

*Connection pool exhaustion.* The app is up, but every database connection or worker thread is busy, so new requests queue and never get serviced. Distinctive symptom: it affects all endpoints at once, including trivial ones, which rules out any single slow query.

*The timeout is just set too low.* Some operation legitimately takes 40 seconds and the gateway is set to 30. Common with exports, bulk imports, and PDF generation.

**How to actually locate it:**

Check whether it's one endpoint or everything. One endpoint points at that code path; everything points at a shared resource — the pool, the database, the host.

Get the timing. If the 504 arrives at exactly 30 or 60 seconds every time, you're hitting a configured timeout, and the round number tells you which layer owns it: different defaults for nginx, ALB, Cloudflare, and so on. If the timing varies, it's more likely load or contention.

Then look at the upstream's own logs for the same request. This is the one that resolves it fastest. If the upstream logged the request as completing in 2 seconds, your problem is between the proxy and the app — networking, or the response being lost. If the upstream never logged completion, the work really is hanging, and now you want to know where: a slow query log, an APM trace, or a thread dump if it's a JVM.

Also worth checking: is there more than one proxy? A CDN in front of a load balancer in front of an ingress in front of the app is four layers with four timeout settings, and a 504 from the outermost one tells you nothing about which of the inner three actually stalled. The response headers usually reveal which layer generated the error.

**The thing 504 does not mean:** it isn't a client problem, and retrying is usually the wrong instinct — if the work is genuinely slow, the retry just adds load to something already struggling, and you can push a degraded service into a full outage that way.

The general shape of this is: never move the table, move the reads and writes. You build the new structure alongside the old one, get both populated, shift traffic across gradually, and delete the old one when you're confident. At 200GB nothing else really works, because any approach involving a lock or a single big transaction will either take hours or blow up your WAL.

**The expand/contract pattern**

This is the standard playbook and it's worth following even when it feels like overkill:

1. **Expand** — create the new schema. New columns, new table, whatever the change is. Additive only, nothing removed, nothing renamed. This step is safe and reversible.
2. **Dual write** — change the application to write to both old and new. Every insert, update, and delete hits both. Deploy this and let it run.
3. **Backfill** — copy the historical rows in batches. This is the long part.
4. **Verify** — compare old and new. Row counts, checksums, spot checks. Take your time here.
5. **Shift reads** — move reads to the new structure, ideally behind a feature flag so you can flip back instantly.
6. **Contract** — once you're confident, stop dual-writing and drop the old table.

The reason for this order is that at every step you can stop and go backwards. Migrations that go badly are usually the ones with a point of no return in the middle.

**On the backfill specifically**

Batch it. Something like 10,000 rows at a time, with a short sleep between batches, keyed on the primary key so you can resume after a failure. Make it idempotent — if it dies at 60% you want to restart it, not start over. Write it so you can adjust the batch size and sleep while it's running, because you'll want to slow it down during peak hours and speed it up overnight.

Watch replication lag while it runs. That's the thing that usually bites: the backfill itself doesn't hurt the primary much, but it generates enough WAL to put your replicas minutes behind, and if you're serving reads off replicas that's a user-visible problem. Lag is the signal to slow down.

Expect this to take days, not hours, and that's fine. It's a background process; there's no prize for finishing fast.

**Postgres-specific things that matter**

If you're adding a column with a default, Postgres 11+ does that without a rewrite. Older versions rewrite the whole table and will lock it — check your version before assuming.

Always build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. A regular `CREATE INDEX` takes a lock that blocks writes for however long it takes on 200GB, which is a long time. Concurrent index builds are slower and can fail, leaving an invalid index you drop and retry — that's fine, it's still the right choice.

Set a short `lock_timeout` on any DDL statement — a second or two. Postgres DDL needs a brief exclusive lock, and if a long-running query is holding a conflicting lock, your `ALTER TABLE` will queue behind it *and every subsequent query will queue behind your ALTER*. That's the classic way a "instant" schema change takes the site down. With a short `lock_timeout` the statement fails fast and you just retry.

Watch your autovacuum. A large backfill creates a lot of dead tuples if it's doing updates, and if autovacuum can't keep up you get bloat and, in the worst case, transaction ID wraparound trouble.

**Alternatives worth knowing about**

If the change is to an existing table's structure rather than a move to a new table, `pg-osc` or `pgroll` automate a lot of this using trigger-based shadow tables. They're solid, and they save you writing the dual-write logic by hand. Worth evaluating before you build it yourself.

If you're actually moving between databases rather than between schemas, logical replication is the better tool — replicate to the new database, let it catch up, then cut over during a brief pause.

**The part people skip**

Verification. Before you shift reads, actually compare the data. Count rows, checksum a sample, and specifically check the rows that changed *during* the backfill, since that's where dual-write bugs hide. And keep the old table around for a while after cutover — disk is cheap, and a table you can still read from is the best rollback plan there is.
